content: A multimeter, also referred to as a multitester or volt/ohm meter (VOM), is an electronic measuring device that integrates multiple functionalities into a single unit. A typical multimeter is capable of measuring voltage, current, and resistance. There are two main types of multimeters: analog multimeters (or analogue multimeters in British English) and digital multimeters (commonly abbreviated as DMM). Multimeters can be handheld devices, suitable for basic troubleshooting and field service tasks, or bench instruments designed for highly accurate measurements. They are widely used to diagnose electrical issues in various industrial and household devices, including batteries, motor controls, appliances, power supplies, and wiring systems. Multimeters are available in a broad range of features and prices, with basic models costing less than $10 and high-end models exceeding $5000. Modern multimeters can measure a variety of quantities, including voltage (in volts), current (in amperes), and resistance (in ohms). Advanced models may also measure capacitance (in farads), frequency (in hertz), duty cycle (as a percentage), temperature (in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit), conductance (in siemens), inductance (in henrys), and audio signal levels (in decibels). Digital multimeters often include additional circuits for continuity testing (with an audible beep when a circuit conducts) and for testing diodes and transistors. Various sensors can be attached to multimeters to measure parameters such as light levels, pH (acidity/alkalinity), wind speed, and relative humidity. The resolution of a digital multimeter is typically specified in terms of digits. For instance, a 5½-digit multimeter displays five full digits (0–9) and one half digit (which can only display 0 or 1). This allows for measurements ranging from 0 to 199,999. A 3¾-digit meter, on the other hand, can display values up to 3,999 or 5,999, depending on the manufacturer. While digital displays can offer high precision, the accuracy of measurements depends on the design and calibration of the analog components within the multimeter. High-resolution measurements require a thorough understanding of the instrument's specifications, careful control of measurement conditions, and traceable calibration. Analog multimeters, in contrast, have their resolution limited by factors such as the width of the scale pointer, pointer vibration, scale printing accuracy, zero calibration, range selection, and errors from non-horizontal use. Resistance measurements on analog meters are particularly imprecise due to the compression of the scale at higher resistance values. Features like mirrored scales and larger meter movements can improve resolution, but analog meters typically achieve a resolution equivalent to 2½ to 3 digits, which is often sufficient for most practical applications. Digital multimeters generally provide more accurate measurements than their analog counterparts. Analog multimeters typically have an accuracy of 3–5%, while laboratory-grade instruments can achieve accuracies in the parts-per-million range. Manufacturers often offer calibration services to ensure that new meters meet traceable standards, such as those set by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Calibration services are also available for older equipment to maintain measurement reliability, especially for critical applications. The sensitivity and input impedance of a multimeter can significantly affect its accuracy. A low current draw from the circuit under test usually results in more precise measurements. Digital multimeters and analog meters with electronic amplifiers typically have high input impedance (often 1–10 million ohms), minimizing circuit disturbance. In contrast, traditional analog meters draw current from the circuit to deflect the pointer, with input impedance varying based on the meter's sensitivity and selected range. For example, a meter with a sensitivity of 20,000 ohms/volt will have an input resistance of 2 million ohms on the 100-volt range. High-sensitivity meters are essential for signal circuits to avoid loading the circuit under test. Alternating current (AC) measurements in multimeters require an AC-to-DC conversion circuit. Basic multimeters use rectifier circuits calibrated to measure the average value of a rectified sine wave, with correction factors provided for certain waveforms. More advanced multimeters include true RMS (root mean square) sensing circuits, which accurately measure the RMS value of various waveforms. RMS sensing is crucial for non-sinusoidal signals, such as those found in audio systems or variable-frequency drives. Modern digital multimeters (DMMs) are preferred for their accuracy, durability, and additional features. In a DMM, the signal under test is converted to a voltage and preconditioned by an amplifier with electronically controlled gain. The measured quantity is displayed as a number, eliminating parallax errors. Features like auto-ranging, auto-polarity, sample-and-hold, and graphical bar displays enhance usability. Some DMMs also include data acquisition capabilities, allowing users to record maximum and minimum readings or take samples at fixed intervals. Advanced models may interface with computers via USB, RS-232, or other communication protocols for data logging and analysis. Analog multimeters, while less common today, are still valued for certain applications. They use a moving-coil galvanometer to deflect a pointer, with sensitivity typically expressed in ohms per volt. High-sensitivity analog meters (e.g., 50,000 ohms/volt) are more delicate but draw minimal current from the circuit under test. Amplified analog meters, such as vacuum tube voltmeters (VTVMs) or transistor voltmeters (TVMs), use amplifiers to achieve high input resistance, reducing circuit loading. Multimeters can utilize various test probes, including crocodile clips, retractable hook clips, and pointed probes, to connect to the circuit under test. High-voltage or high-current measurements may require non-contact probes for safety. Clamp meters, for instance, measure current by clamping around a conductor. Safety features in multimeters include fuses to protect against overloads, though these often only safeguard the highest current range. Digital multimeters are categorized based on their intended application, as defined by the EN 61010 standard. Categories range from I (low current levels) to IV (high current levels, such as service entrances). Category-rated meters also include protections against over-current faults. Multimeters were first invented in the 1920s to support the growing use of vacuum tube electronics. As modern systems become more complex, multimeters have evolved to include advanced features or are supplemented by specialized equipment for specific tasks. For example, while a general-purpose multimeter might test for short circuits and basic insulation quality, modern technicians may use handheld analyzers to validate network cable performance.
